old: Its earliest recorded sense in Old English wasn't the whole thing—just a crumb or broken bit of it.
The Old English word behind it, brēad, once meant simply "morsel," before it came to mean the food itself.
It shares deep roots with German Brot and Dutch brood, all tracing to the same old Germanic word.
clues: A kitchen staple found on tables around the world, its name likely traces back to an ancient root meaning "to boil" or "to brew."
It's baked from flour, water and usually yeast, then sliced for toast or sandwiches. Plainer than cake, it's the food itself, not just one loaf of it.
Its German cousin is Brot, and it completes the phrases "the best thing since sliced ___" and "give us this day our daily ___."
